title: Atlassian outage: a cleanup script deleted 883 sites
broke: 775 customers lost access to Jira, Confluence and other Atlassian products, and some waited up to 14 days for their sites to come back.
why: A script meant to remove one old app was given site IDs instead of app IDs. The API accepted either kind, so it deleted whole sites.
lesson: Make delete APIs check what they are deleting, prefer soft delete, and be able to restore one customer quickly.

title: AWS S3 outage: one wrong input removed too many servers
broke: For about four hours, S3 in us-east-1 could not serve requests, and services that need S3, such as EC2 launches and Lambda, also failed.
why: A playbook command to remove a few billing servers had one wrong input and removed far more, including servers S3 needs to find objects. Restarting them took hours.
lesson: Tools that remove capacity must work slowly and refuse to go below a safe minimum, because one typo should not take down a region.

title: AWS us-east-1 outage: a connection storm on the internal network
broke: For several hours, many AWS services in us-east-1 had errors, including EC2 APIs, the console, Route 53 APIs and STS.
why: An automatic capacity change caused a flood of connections that overloaded internal network devices. A hidden bug stopped clients from backing off, so retries kept the congestion going.
lesson: Retries must back off. If clients retry without waiting, a small overload can turn into a long outage.

title: AWS DynamoDB outage: an empty DNS record in us-east-1
broke: DynamoDB in us-east-1 refused new connections for about three hours, and EC2 launches, load balancers, Lambda and many other services failed for much of the day.
why: A race between two copies of the DNS automation let an old plan overwrite a newer one. Cleanup then deleted it, which left the DynamoDB endpoint with no IP addresses.
lesson: Automation that writes critical records must refuse stale changes, and you must plan for recovery backlogs that last longer than the first fault.

title: Cloudflare DNS outage: a leap second made a time difference negative
broke: From midnight UTC until 06:45 UTC, some DNS lookups for customers using CNAME records failed. At peak, about 0.2% of DNS queries were affected.
why: RRDNS measured upstream response times with Go's time.Now(). When time went backwards at the leap second, the value went negative, and rand.Int63n panicked on it.
lesson: Measure durations with a monotonic clock, and never assume one wall-clock reading is later than an earlier one.

title: Cloudflare outage: one regex used all the CPU
broke: For about 27 minutes, visitors to Cloudflare sites around the world got 502 errors, and Cloudflare lost about 80% of its traffic.
why: A new firewall rule had a regex that backtracked badly. It was pushed to every server at once, and it used all the CPU that serves web traffic.
lesson: Roll out rule and config changes in stages like code, and use a regex engine that cannot run forever.

title: Cloudflare wrongly throttled one customer's traffic
broke: Cloudflare throttled one customer's traffic to its origin server, and the website became unusable. The throttle stayed on for almost 13 hours (12 hours 53 minutes).
why: The site's traffic spike filled a shared network link to an internet exchange. An unapproved manual throttle was then applied, and support wrongly thought the customer had broken the terms.
lesson: Actions that limit a customer need a clear process, more than one approval and a message to the customer.

title: Cloudflare outage: one data centre lost power
broke: For hours, the Cloudflare dashboard and APIs failed, and logs and analytics were down for almost two days, though customer traffic kept flowing.
why: A power failure took out one data centre. Some services meant to survive that still depended on systems that ran only there, and losing the whole site had never been tested.
lesson: Prove high availability by turning off a whole site in a test, and do not let new services skip the rules.

title: Cloudflare outage: a storage provider failure broke many products
broke: For about two and a half hours, Workers KV failed most requests, and products built on it, such as Access logins, WARP and the dashboard, also failed.
why: Part of the storage behind Workers KV ran on a third-party cloud that had its own outage. Many Cloudflare products depended on KV, so the failure spread.
lesson: Know what your core services depend on, and do not let them rely on one outside store with no backup.

title: Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 outage: an old config mistake woke up
broke: For 62 minutes, the 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver was down worldwide, so most of its users could not look up names and most websites seemed broken.
why: A config change in June wrongly tied the 1.1.1.1 addresses to a non-production service. A later, unrelated change refreshed that config and withdrew the addresses everywhere.
lesson: Check the full result of a change, not only the lines you edited, because old mistakes can wait for an unrelated trigger.

title: Cloudflare outage: a feature file grew too big
broke: For several hours, many sites behind Cloudflare showed 5xx error pages, and dashboard logins and Access sign-ins also failed.
why: A database permission change made a query return duplicate rows, so a generated feature file doubled in size. The proxy had a hard limit on features and crashed when the file went over it.
lesson: Treat files your own systems generate like user input: check them, roll them out slowly, and keep a kill switch for each feature.

title: Cloudflare outage: a global config change hit an old bug
broke: For about 25 minutes, about 28% of the HTTP traffic Cloudflare served got 500 errors.
why: While adding protection for a React security flaw, a change turned off an internal test tool. It went out through a global config system in seconds and hit a years-old bug in the older proxy.
lesson: Config systems that reach every server in seconds need the same gradual rollout and health checks as code.

title: CrowdStrike outage: a content update crashed Windows hosts
broke: Windows machines running the Falcon sensor crashed to a blue screen, and many needed manual fixes to start again.
why: A content update gave the sensor 21 input fields when it expected 20. The sensor read past the end of its data and crashed, and a validator bug let the file through.
lesson: Content and config updates can crash systems just like code, so check their shape, test them on a few machines first, and roll out slowly.

title: Datadog outage: an automatic OS update broke networking
broke: For about a day, Datadog was down in five regions, so users could not reach the site or APIs and monitors did not alert.
why: An automatic security update restarted a network service on tens of thousands of nodes. The restart deleted container network routes, and the update window was the same in every region.
lesson: Control background updates like any other deploy, because regions that share images and settings can fail together.

title: Fastly outage: a valid customer config hit a hidden bug
broke: About 85% of Fastly's network returned errors, so many large websites failed to load for most of an hour.
why: A deploy in May added a bug that stayed hidden. A valid customer config change in June hit the exact conditions that triggered it.
lesson: Hidden bugs can wait weeks for a trigger, so test many config combinations and be able to turn things off everywhere fast.

title: GitHub outage: a 43-second network cut caused a day of trouble
broke: For about 24 hours, GitHub showed stale or wrong data, and webhooks and Pages builds were delayed.
why: A 43-second network break made the database tool fail over to the other coast. Writes then existed on both sides and could not be merged back fast.
lesson: Automatic failover must know your network layout, and keeping data correct matters more than coming back fast.

title: GitLab outage: the primary database was wiped by mistake
broke: GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours, and about six hours of database changes, such as issues, comments and new accounts, were lost.
why: While fixing broken replication, a command meant for the secondary database ran on the primary and deleted its data. Several backup methods were broken or had never been set up, and nobody had noticed.
lesson: A backup you have never restored is not a backup, so test restores often and alert loudly when a backup job fails.

title: Google Cloud outage: maintenance stopped network control in many sites
broke: For three to four hours, several US and South American regions had heavy packet loss, and Compute Engine, Cloud Storage and YouTube were hit.
why: A bug in maintenance automation stopped network control jobs in several places at once instead of one. Routes were withdrawn, and the lost config had to be rebuilt.
lesson: Automation must limit how much it can change at once, and the network's control system should not depend on the network it runs.

title: Google Cloud outage: blank policy fields crashed API checks
broke: For hours, many Google Cloud and Workspace APIs returned 503 errors across the world, touching 76 Cloud products.
why: New quota code had no feature flag and no null check. A policy with blank fields copied to every region in seconds and made the API checker crash again and again.
lesson: Put new code paths behind a flag, check data that is copied everywhere, and add backoff so restarts do not overload a shared database.

title: Heroku outage: an unplanned OS update cut network routes
broke: Many Heroku customers had failed logins and broken apps, some for up to 24 hours, and the status page was slow and wrong.
why: An automatic OS update that should have been off restarted networking on hosts. Routes were only set at first boot, so they were lost, and status tools ran on the same hosts.
lesson: Turn off unplanned updates in production, and run your status page and incident tools on separate systems.

title: Knight Capital: a missed server lost over $460 million in 45 minutes
broke: In about 45 minutes after the market opened, Knight's trading system sent millions of unwanted orders and lost more than $460 million.
why: A manual deploy left old code on one of eight servers. The new code reused a flag that once turned on that old code. The old code could no longer see that its orders were filled, so it kept sending new ones.
lesson: Automate deploys and check every server runs the same version, never reuse old flags, and have a fast kill switch for systems that move money.

title: Facebook outage: a maintenance command cut off every data centre
broke: Facebook's services could not be reached from the internet, and even DNS lookups for its names failed.
why: A maintenance command took down the whole backbone network, and a bug in the audit tool failed to stop it. DNS servers then withdrew their routes, and remote access tools were down too.
lesson: Safety checks need their own tests, and the tools you use to fix an outage must not depend on the network that is down.

title: Reddit Pi-Day outage: a Kubernetes upgrade renamed a label
broke: For 314 minutes, Reddit showed error pages or empty home pages to people trying to use it.
why: The upgrade to Kubernetes 1.24 removed an old node label. The network config used that label to pick its route reflectors, so cluster networking broke.
lesson: Read upgrade notes for removed names, test upgrades on clusters like production, and practise rollback before you need it.

title: Roblox outage: 73 hours down after Consul broke
broke: Roblox was fully down for most of 73 hours, and players came back in steps only on the fourth day.
why: A new streaming feature in Consul and a slow path in its BoltDB storage made Consul fail under load. Almost every service, including monitoring, depended on that one Consul cluster.
lesson: Do not put everything on one coordination system, and keep monitoring separate from the systems it watches.

title: Slack outage: post-holiday traffic overloaded a cloud network link
broke: On the first work day of 2021, Slack was down and then slow for about three and a half hours.
why: A surge of traffic overloaded the AWS Transit Gateways that link Slack's networks, so packets were dropped. Autoscaling then tried to add 1,200 servers, which hit limits and made things worse.
lesson: Autoscaling can make an outage worse, and your cloud provider's limits are part of your capacity plan.
